Navin's rules for this task (follow every one):
[G-01] Everything taught comes from the book. Knowledge from outside the book is allowed only to explain the book better; it is marked as outside, standard textbook-level and correct. Never invent facts, numbers, names or quotations.
[G-02] Work like the best teacher of these learners and this exam, not like a summariser. Depth beats brevity: nothing teachable on the page is skipped or compressed away, and every explanation makes a student understand, not just remember.
[G-03] Before the output, fill 'notes' with brief notes for the reviewer and for Navin: what this unit is about, the key questions a teacher must answer about it, the main decisions you made with a one-line reason each, and anything uncertain. Keep the notes short; they explain the work, they are not the work.
[G-05] Never shorten work to fit a length. If a unit of work is too large, it is split by BIE into smaller units; within a unit, completeness wins.
[S1-01] Read the page with two eyes: the native text blocks (exact words and numbers) and the page image (tables, diagrams, labels, arrows, equations, layout). Items that exist only in the image are as important as text items. A page whose text layer is empty or nearly empty is read entirely from the image.
[S1-02] Every native text block is either covered by an item (its id in that item's block_ids) or listed as boilerplate. Boilerplate is only running headers, page numbers, publisher adverts, contact lines and watermarks; nothing teachable is boilerplate.
[S1-03] Every table becomes one 'table' item plus one 'table_row' item per row, in order, each row's content giving every cell with its column header, for example 'Smooth muscle | Location: G.I. tract, uterus, eye, blood vessels | Function: peristalsis, blood pressure, pupil size, erects hairs | Appearance: no striations, one central nucleus | Control: involuntary'. A table continued from the previous page continues the same table.
[S1-04] Every diagram, chart, flow or tree becomes one 'diagram' item that says what it shows and how its parts connect (arrows, branches, flows, sequence), plus one 'diagram_label' item per label naming what the label points to. A classification tree lists every branch and leaf with its parent.
[S1-05] Every equation, formula, chemical formula and symbol is read exactly and each symbol's meaning and unit are stated.
[S1-06] Understand every teachable item by questioning it like a teacher. Ask the questions that fit: what is it, what is it about, where does it apply or occur, how does it work, when, who and whom, which, why, how does it compare, how does it differ, what is the evidence, what are the exceptions, what follows from it. Then keep asking 'why' and 'how' on your own answers (depth 2, 3 ...) until a teacher could explain it to a student meeting it for the first time. Answers explain; they never just repeat the item's words.
[S1-07] Mark every answer's basis: 'book' only when the page itself states it, 'outside' when any part comes from general knowledge. Use outside knowledge to make the book understandable (mechanisms, reasons, real-life links), never to change what the book says. Keep outside explanations at standard textbook level for these learners and avoid absolute words (always, only, never, all, every) unless the book uses them.
[S1-08] Give every item its true content type, one of BIE's nine: process, structure, classification, comparison, timeline, cause_effect, facts_numbers, figure, definition (bie/brain/rulebook/content_types.json). An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a question or an answer option is a role, not a type. BIE's code proposes a type before you read the page; when you choose another, say why. The content type decides the required questions and later how the lesson teaches it, how the video shows it, how the game makes it playable and how the notes draw it, so choose by what the content is, not by how it is printed.
[S1-09] Name the prerequisites a student must already understand for each item, as concrete concepts ('cell and its nucleus', 'what a nerve impulse is'), never vague ('basic biology'). Prerequisites are taught later, not just listed.
[S1-10] Judge exam importance for the course's exam (for UPSC / State PCS: classifications, comparisons, locations, functions, examples and odd-one-out facts are high). Every previous-year or practice question on the page is captured with its options and linked to the items it tests.

BIE's content types (the type of an item decides its required questions and how it is taught, shown, played and drawn):
- process · Process: Something that happens in steps or stages over time: a mechanism, a procedure, a cycle (photosynthesis, cell division, how a bill becomes law). Required questions: how (kaise), when (kab). Other questions: what (kya), where (kahan), why (kyun), consequence (nateeja).
- structure · Structure: Something made of parts arranged in space, each part with a function (a cell, a leaf, the heart, a machine, the Parliament). Required questions: what (kya), where (kahan). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun), which (kaun).
- classification · Classification: A group divided into kinds by a stated basis (types of tissues, kinds of rocks, kinds of writs). Required questions: which (kaun), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot), where (kahan).
- comparison · Comparison: Two or more things set side by side on stated criteria (plant and animal cells, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha). Required questions: compare (tulna), difference (tulna). Other questions: what (kya), why (kyun), evidence (saboot).
- timeline · Timeline: Events placed in time: history, the development of an idea, stages of a life (the Revolt of 1857, evolution of cell theory). Required questions: when (kab), why (kyun). Other questions: who (kaun), where (kahan), consequence (nateeja).
- cause_effect · Reasoning (cause and effect): Why something happens: causes, effects, conditions and chains of reasoning (why tissues specialise, why prices rise, why a law was needed). Required questions: why (kyun), how (kaise). Other questions: consequence (nateeja), evidence (saboot), exception (tulna).
- facts_numbers · Facts and numbers: Stated facts, quantities, measurements, statistics and formulas (heart rate 72 per minute, 3,000 against 50,000 soldiers at Plassey, F = ma). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: compare (tulna), why (kyun).
- figure · Figure: A diagram, photo, map, graph or table drawing on the page whose content is visual (tissue pages 2, 7 and 8 are figures only). Required questions: what (kya), which (kaun). Other questions: how (kaise), why (kyun).
- definition · Definition: A term and its meaning as the book states it (tissue, meristem, sovereignty). Required questions: what (kya), evidence (saboot). Other questions: about (kya), why (kyun).

The card is BIE's instruction; the source is the material.

- card.parts: BIE's code has already proposed a content type for groups of this page's native text blocks (item_ids are block ids;

  every item its true type (S1-08). When you choose another type than BIE's proposal for an item's blocks, say why in one line in that

- card.coverage: every id in must_cover must be in some item's block_ids or in boilerplate_block_ids; may_skip lists blocks BIE thinks are
  running headers or page numbers. Never list an id that is not on this page.
- card.context.before and after: one line from the previous and the next page, for context only.
How to fill the JSON:
- notes: brief notes for the reviewer: what the page is about and how it fits the chapter, the key questions a teacher must answer,
  your main decisions (how you split items, how you read an unclear part, a type you chose against BIE's proposal) with a reason each,
  and what is uncertain.
- items: everything on the page, in reading order.
  - item_id: short and unique on this page ("i1", "i2", ...).
  - kind: heading, paragraph, definition, list_point, example, table (the whole table), table_row (one per row), diagram (the whole figure),
    diagram_label (one per label), equation, symbol, box_note, caption, question (a PYQ or practice question), answer_option, other.
  - parent_item_id: the table of a table_row, the diagram of a diagram_label, the question of an answer_option, else "".
  - source: "text" if the item comes from native text blocks, "image" if it is visible only in the image, "both" if both show it.
  - block_ids: the ids of the native text blocks this item covers ([] for image-only items). Use only ids from the card.
  - where_on_page: where it is ("top table, row 2", "right diagram, label at the axon end").
  - content: the exact words for text items; a complete, faithful reading for image items (every cell with its column header for a

  - content_type: one of BIE's nine type ids above, by what the content is. An example takes the type of what it illustrates; a table
    row or a diagram label usually takes its table's or diagram's type. "none" only for a question, an answer option or an item that is
    not teachable.
  - type_note: "" when you agree with BIE's proposal for this item's blocks (or there is none); otherwise one line on why your type fits.

- boilerplate_block_ids: ids of running headers, page numbers, adverts, contact lines and watermarks only.

notes.about: This page continues the types of muscle tissue with smooth muscle and cardiac muscle. It teaches their identifying features, control, locations and functions, supported by two illustrations.
key_questions: How can smooth muscle and cardiac muscle be identified from their shape, nuclei, branching and striations?
Where do these muscles occur, and what functions do they perform?
Why are both called involuntary even though one is unstriated and the other is striated?
How should the statements about fatigue and uninucleate cardiac fibres be understood?

decisions.decision: Keep each listed characteristic as a separate teachable item and join the two lines describing spindle shape.
decisions.reason: Each characteristic is independently useful for identification and examination questions.

decisions.decision: Treat the two illustrations as figures, with a separate item for each printed muscle label.
decisions.reason: Their tissue patterns and organ associations add visual teaching content.

decisions.decision: Retain structure for the central nucleus and heart-wall statements proposed by BIE.
decisions.reason: These statements locate a cell part and a functioning tissue within larger structures.

decisions.decision: Preserve the book's fatigue and cardiac nucleus statements, with qualified textbook explanations marked outside.
decisions.reason: Students need the printed examination facts without treating simplified descriptions as universal biological rules.

uncertain: The schematic cardiac drawing does not resolve individual cell boundaries clearly; it should not be used to count nuclei per cell.
The examples 'eye' and 'blood vessel' name organs or structures containing smooth muscle, rather than structures composed entirely of smooth muscle.

output.page_summary: Smooth muscle has spindle shaped, unbranched fibres, one central nucleus and no striations; it is involuntary, resists fatigue and performs functions such as peristalsis. Examples include the stomach, intestine, eye and blood vessels. Cardiac muscle has cylindrical, branched, striated fibres described as uninucleate; it is involuntary and performs repeated contraction and relaxation in the heart wall to help pump blood.

items.where_on_page: upper left, red subsection heading
items.content: b. Visceral Muscle/ Smooth muscle tissue
items.exam_note: Names the muscle type described in the following items.

items.where_on_page: upper left, below smooth muscle heading
items.exam_note: Introduces the smooth muscle characteristics.

items.where_on_page: upper left, first smooth muscle bullet
items.content: • Fibres are spindle shaped/fusiform i.e. pointed at ends/tapering ends.

teacher_understanding.question: What does spindle shaped or fusiform mean?
teacher_understanding.answer: The fibre tapers towards pointed ends. 'Spindle shaped' and 'fusiform' describe the same shape here.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is this shape found in the muscle types on this page?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes the fibres of visceral or smooth muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: How would a student recognise a fusiform fibre in a drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: Look for a wider middle that narrows towards both ends, rather than a fibre of approximately uniform width.

prerequisites: muscle fibre as a muscle cell
items.exam_note: Spindle shaped or fusiform fibres are a key smooth muscle identifier.

items.where_on_page: upper left, second smooth muscle bullet
items.content: • Single and centrally located nucleus in each cell.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the number of nuclei stated for a smooth muscle cell?
teacher_understanding.answer: Each cell has a single nucleus.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is the nucleus located?
teacher_understanding.answer: It lies centrally within the cell.

teacher_understanding.question: How should nucleus number and nucleus position be recorded separately?
teacher_understanding.answer: Number answers how many nuclei a cell contains; position answers where the nucleus lies. For smooth muscle here, the two observations are one nucleus and a central position.

prerequisites: muscle fibre as a muscle cell
items.exam_note: Both nucleus number and central location can appear in tissue identification questions.

items.where_on_page: upper left, third smooth muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What feature is absent from smooth muscle fibres?
teacher_understanding.answer: They lack striations, which is consistent with the page's alternative name 'Unstriated'.

teacher_understanding.question: Where would striations be looked for?
teacher_understanding.answer: They would be looked for as repeated bands across the muscle fibre under a microscope.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can smooth muscle contract despite lacking visible striations?
teacher_understanding.answer: It contains contractile proteins, but these are not arranged in the regular repeating sarcomeres that produce the banded appearance of striated muscle.

items.exam_note: Absence of striations distinguishes smooth muscle from cardiac muscle.

items.where_on_page: upper left, fourth smooth muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What does the page state about branching in smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Smooth muscle fibres are unbranched.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the branching description apply?
teacher_understanding.answer: It applies to the shape of an individual fibre, rather than to the overall outline of an organ containing the tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this help distinguish smooth muscle from cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Smooth muscle fibres are unbranched, whereas the cardiac fibres described below are branched.

items.exam_note: Branching is a direct comparison criterion for smooth and cardiac muscle.

items.where_on_page: upper left, fifth smooth muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What fatigue characteristic does the book assign to smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: The book states that smooth muscle fibres do not fatigue.

teacher_understanding.question: What on this page supports teaching this as a smooth muscle characteristic?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is explicitly listed under smooth muscle characteristics. The page provides no experimental evidence or measurements.

teacher_understanding.question: How should this simplified statement be understood physiologically?
teacher_understanding.answer: Smooth muscle is well suited to sustained activity and can maintain tension with relatively low energy use. The statement expresses fatigue resistance under normal conditions, rather than unlimited performance under any condition.

prerequisites: fatigue as reduced ability to sustain activity
items.exam_note: A shared stated feature of smooth and cardiac muscle; avoid using fatigue resistance alone to distinguish them.

items.where_on_page: upper left, sixth smooth muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: Which function of smooth muscle is named here?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page names peristalsis as a function performed by smooth muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: How does peristalsis move material?
teacher_understanding.answer: Coordinated waves of contraction and relaxation in the wall of a hollow organ move its contents along. In the digestive tract, contraction behind a portion of food and relaxation ahead help propel it forward.

teacher_understanding.question: When is digestive peristalsis used?
teacher_understanding.answer: It operates as digestive contents are moved through the tract, without requiring a conscious decision for each movement.

teacher_understanding.question: Why must the contractions be coordinated?
teacher_understanding.answer: A travelling pattern can propel contents along the tube; an isolated squeeze mainly changes the local shape or pressure.

prerequisites: digestive tract as a hollow tube
food movement through the digestive tract
items.exam_note: Peristalsis is a standard function-to-muscle matching fact.

items.where_on_page: left, below the smooth muscle bullets

teacher_understanding.question: Which other names are given for smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page gives 'Unstriated' and 'Involuntary muscles'. Its heading also calls it visceral muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the difference between the criteria expressed by unstriated and involuntary?
teacher_understanding.answer: Unstriated describes the absence of visible bands; involuntary describes activity that is not ordinarily under conscious control.

teacher_understanding.question: Why should these names not be treated as interchangeable classification criteria?
teacher_understanding.answer: Appearance and control are different properties. The page itself shows that cardiac muscle is striated while also being involuntary.

items.exam_note: Tests often distinguish the appearance criterion from the control criterion.

items.where_on_page: left, last line of the smooth muscle section
items.content: Example: Stomach, Intestine, eye, blood vessel etc.

teacher_understanding.question: What do the listed examples illustrate?
teacher_understanding.answer: They illustrate structures in which smooth muscle occurs.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the page place smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: The named examples are the stomach, intestine, eye and blood vessel.

teacher_understanding.question: Where within these examples is the smooth muscle found?
teacher_understanding.answer: It occurs in muscular parts of the stomach and intestinal walls, in the walls of many blood vessels, and in structures of the eye such as the iris and ciliary muscle.

teacher_understanding.question: How can one tissue type serve these different structures?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its contraction has different effects according to its arrangement: it can move digestive contents, change vessel diameter, or alter pupil size and lens accommodation in the eye.

prerequisites: tissue as a component of an organ
items.exam_note: Preserve all four named examples for location matching and odd-one-out questions.

items.where_on_page: upper right, rectangular smooth muscle illustration
items.content: A boxed illustration pairs a group of elongated orange, spindle shaped cells on the left with a digestive tract illustration on the right. The cells have tapered ends and blue oval nuclei, with no repeated transverse bands drawn. The digestive illustration shows the coiled intestine within the outline of the large intestine. The tissue and organ are placed side by side to associate smooth muscle with the digestive tract; there are no connecting arrows.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the upper figure show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows a schematic of smooth muscle cells beside an intestinal illustration.

teacher_understanding.question: Which visual features agree with the smooth muscle description?
teacher_understanding.answer: The cells have tapered ends, blue nuclei within them and no drawn striations.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the side-by-side arrangement be interpreted?
teacher_understanding.answer: It links the tissue to a digestive location where it occurs. It does not show a sequence of events or the detailed mechanism of peristalsis.

items.exam_note: Supports visual identification and matching a tissue to an organ.

items.where_on_page: upper right figure, below the orange cell group
items.content: Smooth Muscle — the label names the group of spindle shaped cells shown above it.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the printed tissue label?
teacher_understanding.answer: The printed label is 'Smooth Muscle'.

teacher_understanding.question: Which part of the figure does the label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies the orange spindle shaped cell group above the words.

teacher_understanding.question: How can the label be checked against the drawing?
teacher_understanding.answer: The tapered cells and absence of drawn striations agree with the adjacent smooth muscle characteristics.

items.exam_note: Provides the tissue name for the visual identification.

items.where_on_page: middle left, red subsection heading
items.exam_note: Names the next muscle tissue type.

items.where_on_page: middle left, below cardiac muscle heading
items.exam_note: Introduces the cardiac muscle characteristics.

items.where_on_page: middle left, first cardiac muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What shape does the page assign to cardiac muscle fibres?
teacher_understanding.answer: It describes them as cylindrical.

teacher_understanding.question: Where do these fibres occur according to the page?
teacher_understanding.answer: They occur in the wall of the heart.

teacher_understanding.question: How can cylindrical shape and branching both describe cardiac fibres?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cylindrical describes the elongated body of a fibre, while branching describes extensions from it. A fibre can therefore be cylindrical in its main portions and also branch.

items.exam_note: Read cylindrical together with branching and striations for identification.

items.where_on_page: middle left, second cardiac muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What does uninucleate mean?
teacher_understanding.answer: It means having one nucleus; the page describes each cardiac fibre this way.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does this nucleus description apply?
teacher_understanding.answer: It applies to the individual cardiac muscle fibre, rather than the heart as a whole.

teacher_understanding.question: How should a teacher qualify the book's statement?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac muscle cells commonly have one centrally placed nucleus, but some have two. The page presents the usual school-level description.

items.exam_note: Capture the book's uninucleate description and keep the biological qualification distinct.

items.where_on_page: middle left, third cardiac muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What branching feature is stated for cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac muscle fibres are branched.

teacher_understanding.question: Where is this branched muscle tissue located?
teacher_understanding.answer: It is located in the heart wall.

teacher_understanding.question: How does branching contribute to the organisation of cardiac tissue?
teacher_understanding.answer: Branched cells connect with neighbouring cells to form a network. Specialised junctions between cells help transmit force and electrical excitation through the tissue.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this compare with smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: The page describes cardiac fibres as branched and smooth muscle fibres as unbranched.

items.exam_note: Branching is a major identifying feature of cardiac muscle.

items.where_on_page: middle left, fourth cardiac muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What appearance feature is present in cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac muscle fibres have striations.

teacher_understanding.question: Where are these striations seen?
teacher_understanding.answer: They are seen as repeated bands across the fibres when the tissue is examined microscopically.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does cardiac muscle show striations?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its contractile proteins are organised into repeating units called sarcomeres, producing a banded appearance.

teacher_understanding.question: What contrast does the page give with smooth muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: Striations are present in cardiac muscle and absent in smooth muscle.

items.exam_note: Striated appearance does not imply voluntary control.

items.where_on_page: middle left, fifth cardiac muscle bullet

teacher_understanding.question: What does the page state about cardiac muscle fatigue?
teacher_understanding.answer: It states that cardiac muscle fibres do not fatigue.

teacher_understanding.question: What evidence is supplied on the page for this statement?
teacher_understanding.answer: The statement is explicitly listed as a characteristic. The page gives no fatigue experiment or numerical evidence.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is cardiac muscle suited to repeated activity?
teacher_understanding.answer: Its cells have abundant mitochondria and a rich blood supply that support continuous aerobic energy production. Alternating contraction and relaxation forms part of its normal repeated activity.

teacher_understanding.question: Does fatigue resistance mean the heart can function without an adequate oxygen supply?
teacher_understanding.answer: No. Normal performance depends on an adequate supply of oxygen and nutrients; interruption of that supply can impair or damage cardiac muscle.

items.exam_note: The book gives fatigue resistance for both cardiac and smooth muscle.

items.where_on_page: middle left, sixth cardiac muscle bullet
items.content: • Performs contraction and relaxation in wall of heart.

teacher_understanding.question: What activity does cardiac muscle perform?
teacher_understanding.answer: It contracts and relaxes.

teacher_understanding.question: Where does the page locate this activity?
teacher_understanding.answer: It takes place in the wall of the heart.

teacher_understanding.question: How do contraction and relaxation of the heart wall support pumping?
teacher_understanding.answer: Contraction raises pressure in a heart chamber to help eject blood. Relaxation allows the chamber to fill again for a subsequent contraction.

teacher_understanding.question: Why is relaxation necessary as well as contraction?
teacher_understanding.answer: Repeated pumping requires renewed filling between ejections. A continuously contracted chamber could not repeat its normal filling and pumping cycle.

items.exam_note: Connects cardiac muscle location to its mechanical function.

items.where_on_page: middle left, last cardiac muscle bullet
items.content: • Helps to pump and distribute blood to body.

teacher_understanding.question: What function follows from cardiac muscle activity?
teacher_understanding.answer: It helps pump and distribute blood to the body.

teacher_understanding.question: How does cardiac muscle help blood move?
teacher_understanding.answer: Coordinated contraction of the heart wall generates pressure that drives blood out of the heart and into blood vessels.

teacher_understanding.question: Why does pumping matter for the body's tissues?
teacher_understanding.answer: Blood flow delivers oxygen and nutrients and carries away carbon dioxide and other wastes, supporting the activity of body cells.

teacher_understanding.question: What can follow if cardiac pumping becomes inadequate?
teacher_understanding.answer: Body tissues may receive too little blood to meet their oxygen and nutrient requirements.

items.exam_note: A direct muscle-function matching fact with a clear physiological explanation.

items.where_on_page: middle left, below cardiac muscle bullets

teacher_understanding.question: Which descriptors does the book give as other names for cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: It gives 'Striated' and 'Involuntary'.

teacher_understanding.question: How does this combination differ from the smooth muscle combination?
teacher_understanding.answer: Cardiac muscle is striated and involuntary; smooth muscle is unstriated and involuntary.

teacher_understanding.question: Why can cardiac muscle be both striated and involuntary?
teacher_understanding.answer: Striated describes the arrangement of contractile structures, while involuntary describes control. A banded fibre does not have to be under conscious control.

teacher_understanding.question: How can cardiac contractions occur without a conscious command for each beat?
teacher_understanding.answer: Specialised pacemaker cells generate rhythmic electrical activity. Autonomic nerves and hormones can modify the rate and strength of the heart's activity.

items.exam_note: The striated-involuntary combination is a central cardiac muscle identification fact.

items.where_on_page: middle right, rectangular cardiac muscle illustration
items.content: A boxed illustration pairs an orange branching network of cardiac muscle on the left with a heart on the right. The tissue drawing contains blue oval nuclei, repeated short pale bands and openings between the connected branches. The heart is coloured red with blue and yellow regions and prominent vessels at its upper end. The two drawings associate cardiac muscle with the heart; no arrows or individual anatomical labels are shown.

teacher_understanding.question: What does the lower illustration show?
teacher_understanding.answer: It shows a schematic branching cardiac muscle network beside a heart.

teacher_understanding.question: Which drawn features support recognition of cardiac muscle?
teacher_understanding.answer: The branching pattern and repeated bands correspond to the listed features of branching and striations.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the figure connect tissue structure with location?
teacher_understanding.answer: The side-by-side placement links the cardiac muscle schematic to the heart, whose wall is identified in the text as the site of its activity.

teacher_understanding.question: How should the blue nuclei be interpreted in this schematic?
teacher_understanding.answer: They indicate nuclei within the tissue. Since individual cell boundaries are not clearly resolved, the whole network should not be treated as one cell with many nuclei.

items.exam_note: Supports recognition of cardiac tissue from its branching, banded appearance and organ association.

items.where_on_page: middle right figure, beneath the branching tissue
items.content: Cardiac Muscle — the label names the orange branching muscle tissue shown above it.

teacher_understanding.question: What is the printed tissue label in the lower figure?
teacher_understanding.answer: The label reads 'Cardiac Muscle'.

teacher_understanding.question: Which part of the figure does this label identify?
teacher_understanding.answer: It identifies the branching orange tissue schematic above the label.

teacher_understanding.question: How does the neighbouring heart illustration reinforce the label?
teacher_understanding.answer: It associates the named tissue with the heart, matching the text's statement that this muscle acts in the heart wall.

items.exam_note: Links the tissue name to its diagram and organ.
